name: Humayun's Tomb
scope: Main mausoleum, raised terrace, white dome, corner chhatris and arched red-sandstone elevations; exclude separate garden tombs and gates.
era: surviving exterior represented by selected dated references

review.method: Qualla-first corpus search,then actual inspection of three native creator-uploaded CC0 originals with first-revision creator grants and exact native hashes.
review.notes: Three2024/2026 originals support sandstone/marble exterior,deep iwans,roof kiosks,17bay terrace,clipped lower platform and corner access steps. Hidden upper stairs follow primary text;dimensions remain architectural estimates. Terrain acceptance is held separately.

candidates.caption:
Humayun's Tomb (Persian: Maqbara-i Humayun) is located in Delhi, India, and serves as the final resting place of Humayun. Empress Bega Begum, his first wife and chief consort, commissioned the tomb in 1558 and selected Persian architects Mirak Mirza Ghiyas and his son, Sayyid Muhammad, for its design. Notably, it was among the earliest structures to utilize red sandstone extensively. In 1993, Humayun's Tomb earned UNESCO World Heritage Site status and has since undergone a thorough restoration, which is now complete. 
This garden-tomb is significant as the first of its kind in the Indian subcontinent and is situated in Nizamuddin East, Delhi, near the Dina-panah Citadel, also known as Purana Qila (Old Fort), founded by Humayun in 1538.

However, it's essential for viewers to understand that capturing images of famous monuments can be extremely challenging. These sites are often crowded with visitors ( including international tourists ) as soon as the gates open, making it difficult to create clean and clear images in the presence of crowds.

Believed to be the residence of patron saint of Delhi, Nizamuddin Auliya (d. 1325), is located just outside the main complex, near the northeastern corner of the principal mausoleum and is an example of Tughlaq period architecture

Nila Gumbad (Blue Dome), Delhi, post restoration. Built ca 1625, by Abdul Rahim Khan-I-Khana, son of Bairam Khan also a courtier in Mughal Emperor, Akbar's court, for his servant Miyan Fahim. Fahim, who not only grew up with his son, but later also died alongside one of Rahim's own sons, Feroze khan, while fighting against the rebellion of Mughal general Mahabat Khan in 1625/26, during the reign of Jahangir.

originalReview.inspection: Upper-deck close oblique: clipped mausoleum,deep pointed iwans,white marble inlay,low dome support,open chhatris and blue roof kiosks.
Whole exterior from garden corner:17bay upper plinth,low stone base,narrow lower walk,central stair niche and dome silhouette.
Full clipped corner from garden level:lower diagonal six-step flight,grey block base,narrow walk,corner door,terrace arcades and full mausoleum.
